subtype: Approach: comparing with others without context [Pitfall]
passage: Class teacher's note, Friday. Hrithik (Class 12) stayed behind after the bell. He said his friend studies fourteen hours every day and he is managing only eight, “so I'm failing.” Last week he tried nine hours and still felt behind; at ten, the same. I pointed out that his friend reads much faster and, as Hrithik himself mentioned, was often unwell last term and is catching up on a different plan. Hrithik looked startled. “I never thought of that.” I asked him to write down his own results across three weeks in place of anyone else's hours. I will check in with him on Monday. — Aparna

qa.q: How many hours a day does Hrithik's friend study?
What did Hrithik feel when he compared himself with his friend?
qa.a: Perpetually behind and inadequate: even at longer hours he felt the same.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do instead of comparing hours, and why?
qa.a: He could track his own results against his earlier ones, because that shows real change without ignoring differences in speed and health.

qa.q: How might the comparison look from the friend's side?
qa.a: The friend may not realise Hrithik measures himself against fourteen hours, and the friend's pace and health differ, so that number may not mean what Hrithik thinks.

grounding: A student measures himself against a friend's fourteen-hour routine, ignoring differences in speed and health, and feels behind.

subtype: Approach: comparing with others without context [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday night

Tarun posted his study log again today. "14 hours ✅". Every single day. And every single day I look at mine, eight hours on a good day, and feel sick.

I'm Santosh, and I have a rule that I'm behind. It doesn't matter what I do. Today I did two full mock papers and my score went up by six marks. But then I saw Tarun's post and it didn't feel like anything.

Mom says, "You're a different boy from Tarun." He reads twice as fast as me, and he doesn't take the bus for an hour each way like I do. And last year he pushed so hard he fell ill and missed a month. I know all that. But when I see "14 hours", my brain deletes it.

I'm tired of feeling like a failure even on days I do well. Maybe I should stop looking at his posts. Maybe I should look at my own graph instead.

qa.q: How many hours does Tarun post that he studies every day?
How does Santosh feel when looking at Tarun's posts?
qa.a: Santosh feels sick and inadequate, like a failure, even on good days.

qa.q: What would you advise Santosh to try first?
qa.a: Stop checking Tarun's log for a while and track progress against Santosh's own past scores, since speed, travel and health differ so much.

qa.q: How might Santosh's mom see the comparison?
qa.a: She probably feels worried and frustrated, knowing the differences between the two boys and wishing Santosh could see them too.

grounding: A diary shows a student comparing himself with a friend who studies fourteen hours a day, ignoring differences in speed and health, and feeling always behind.
